**How to use this lecture.** Download the R script, open it in RStudio and run it line by line (Cmd+Enter on a Mac, Ctrl+Enter on Windows). All explanations on this page are in the script as comments. Check that you get the same output as shown here. Quiz 1 asks you to read and interpret exactly this kind of code and output.

[Download the R script](../materials/ski3011/week-2/r-lecture-2.R){.btn .btn-primary} [Download the practice file bcg.csv](../materials/ski3011/week-2/bcg.csv){.btn .btn-outline-primary}



## Why R?

R is a program for statistical computing, not just for meta-analyses. To learn to do a meta-analysis in R, we first need the basics. A general principle of responsible research: keep only two files, the raw data file and the script. Never change the raw data by hand without logging it: every change is a line in the script.

## R as a calculator


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
4 + 3
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 7
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
4 * 2
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 8
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
4^2
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 16
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
log(4)    # natural logarithm
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 1.386294
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
exp(4)    # the inverse of log()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 54.59815
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
sqrt(4)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 2
```


:::
:::


## Vectors and functions

A vector combines values that belong together, like a column in a spreadsheet: the ages of participants, or the effect sizes of the studies in a meta-analysis. `c()` stands for combine. A function such as `mean()` takes arguments between brackets. Use `?` to open the help page of a function.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
c(9, 3, 6)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 9 3 6
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
mean(c(9, 3, 6))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 6
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
sd(c(9, 3, 6))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 3
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
sort(c(9, 3, 6), decreasing = TRUE)   # an extra argument changes what the function does
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 9 6 3
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# ?sort                               # remove the # to open the help page
```
:::


## Objects

A vector, a dataset or a single value can be stored in an object with `<-`. You choose the name yourself. The object appears in the Environment window (top right in RStudio).


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
a <- c(9, 3, 6)
a
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 9 3 6
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
b <- 2 + 2
a / b      # every value of a is divided by b
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 2.25 0.75 1.50
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
z <- a / b
z
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 2.25 0.75 1.50
```


:::
:::


## Data frames

A data frame is a table: one row per study, one column per variable. Here we make the meta-analysis dataset you know from SKI3010 by hand: 11 studies on environmental tobacco smoke at home and bladder cancer, with the log odds ratio and its standard error.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
lnOR <- c(-0.223143551, -0.198450939, -0.162518929, -0.162518929, -0.116533816, 0.009950331,
          0.086177696, 0.139761942, 0.165514438, 0.336472237, 0.457424847)
se <- c(0.38457745, 0.301271952, 0.200831965, 0.279480271, 0.359347184, 0.428673775,
        0.247347883, 0.162072911, 0.251023247, 0.3350916, 0.293754916)
firstauthor <- c("Alberg (2)", "Bjerregaard", "Jiang", "Burch", "NLCS", "Kabat",
                 "Baris", "Zheng", "Samanic", "Alberg (1)", "Tao")
year <- c(2007, 2006, 2007, 1989, 2002, 1986, 2009, 2012, 2006, 2007, 2010)
dat <- data.frame(firstauthor, year, lnOR, se)
dat
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}


## Reading a csv file

Most of your data will come from a spreadsheet saved as csv. Download the practice file bcg.csv and put it in the folder where you keep your script. `getwd()` shows the folder R works in; in RStudio you can change it via Session, Set Working Directory, To Source File Location.

European csv files use a semicolon as separator and a comma as decimal sign. If you forget that, R reads everything into one column:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# getwd()                    # which folder is R working in?
wrong <- read.csv("bcg.csv")
head(wrong, 2)               # one column, everything glued together
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
                                        author.year.tpos.tneg.cpos.cneg.ablat.risk_vaccinated
Aronson;1948;4;119;11;128;44;0                                                            325
Ferguson & Simes;1949;6;300;29;274;55;0                                                   196
```


:::
:::


Tell R which separator and decimal sign the file uses:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
bcg <- read.csv("bcg.csv", sep = ";", dec = ",")
head(bcg, 3)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
            author year tpos tneg cpos cneg ablat risk_vaccinated
1          Aronson 1948    4  119   11  128    44          0.0325
2 Ferguson & Simes 1949    6  300   29  274    55          0.0196
3  Rosenthal et al 1960    3  228   11  209    42          0.0130
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
dim(bcg)        # number of rows (studies) and columns (variables)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 13  8
```


:::
:::


## Data types

R distinguishes numeric values (for calculations), logical values (TRUE or FALSE), character values (text) and factors (categories). `class()` tells you which type an object is.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
a <- 44 / 5
class(a)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "numeric"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
b <- 7 > 4
b
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] TRUE
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
class(b)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "logical"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
class(bcg$author)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "character"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
pets <- c("cat", "dog", "cat", "bird", "cat")
class(pets)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "character"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
pets <- as.factor(pets)   # a factor: a categorical variable with levels
levels(pets)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "bird" "cat"  "dog" 
```


:::
:::


## Some simple statistics

R has built-in datasets. `airquality` contains daily air measurements in New York. Does ozone concentration depend on temperature? In `lm()` the tilde `~` separates the outcome from the explanatory variable.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
dim(airquality)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 153   6
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
head(airquality, 3)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
  Ozone Solar.R Wind Temp Month Day
1    41     190  7.4   67     5   1
2    36     118  8.0   72     5   2
3    12     149 12.6   74     5   3
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
fit <- lm(Ozone ~ Temp, data = airquality)
summary(fit)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}


## Plots

The built-in dataset `iris` has flower measurements of three species. Arguments such as `main`, `xlab`, `pch` and `col` change the title, axis labels, symbols and colours.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
hist(iris$Petal.Length, main = "Histogram of petal length", xlab = "Petal length")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](r-lecture-2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
boxplot(Petal.Length ~ Species, data = iris,
        main = "Petal length by species", xlab = "Species", ylab = "Petal length")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](r-lecture-2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
plot(iris$Petal.Length, iris$Sepal.Length, pch = 20, col = "darkorange",
     main = "Petal length and sepal length", xlab = "Petal length", ylab = "Sepal length")
abline(lm(Sepal.Length ~ Petal.Length, data = iris))   # add the regression line
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](r-lecture-2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


## Saving your data

`write.csv()` saves a data frame as a csv file in your working directory; `read.csv()` reads it back. This line is not run on the website.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
write.csv(bcg, "my_bcg_data.csv", row.names = FALSE)
my_data <- read.csv("my_bcg_data.csv")
```
:::


## Now your own data

Import your own extraction sheet (saved as csv) with `read.csv()` and check it with `head()`, `dim()` and `class()`.
